planting.note: Root stem cuttings or divisions in spring after frost danger passes, in gritty cactus mix in bright light with afternoon shade in hot climates; allow cut surfaces to callus for a few days before potting.

directions: Stapelia grandiflora is a mat-forming South African succulent with soft, four-angled, toothed stems that root wherever they touch soil, spreading slowly into low clumps. Its huge star-shaped flowers, sometimes reaching 10 inches across, are edged in fine white hairs surrounding a center tufted with purple hairs, and they give off a faint carrion scent that draws fly pollinators. Grow it in bright light with some afternoon shade in the hottest regions, in an extremely fast-draining cactus mix, and let the soil dry fully between waterings to avoid stem rot. Reduce watering further in winter while the plant rests.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
San Marcos Growers
Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring after frost danger passes, in gritty cactus mix in bright, filtered light; let cut ends callus for a few days before inserting into the rooting medium.

directions: Stapelia hirsuta is a low, clumping South African succulent with soft-toothed, four-angled stems and deep maroon to rusty-red flowers covered in fine hair, giving the blooms a shaggy, almost fur-covered texture. The five-pointed blossoms mimic the look and smell of decaying flesh, a scent strategy aimed at flies rather than bees or butterflies. It prefers bright, filtered light such as morning sun with afternoon shade, and a gritty cactus mix that dries out completely between waterings. Withhold water almost entirely in winter and keep it above 50°F to prevent stem collapse.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
World of Succulents
San Marcos Growers

planting.note: Break off a rooted offset or stem section, let it callus for a day or two, then set it shallowly in a very gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright, indirect light; established clumps can also be divided.

directions: Huernia schneideriana forms clustering, upright stems edged with soft, thorn-like tubercles that are surprisingly harmless to the touch, gradually sprawling or trailing as the clump matures. Its star-shaped flowers open a deep burgundy-red with a fleshy texture, adding rich color to a genus mostly known for paler, banded blooms. Give it bright, indirect light with only brief direct sun, since strong midday exposure can scorch the stems, and let the gritty succulent mix dry out completely between waterings. Its trailing habit as it ages makes it well suited to shallow pots and hanging containers.
sources: San Marcos Growers
Cactus and Succulent Society of America
University of California Cooperative Extension — Succulents

planting.note: Break off a rooted offset or stem section, allow it to callus briefly, then set shallowly in a very gritty, fast-draining succulent mix in bright light with some midday shade; mature clumps also divide easily.

directions: Huernia pillansii is one of the most distinct species in the genus, covered in soft, bristly, hair-like projections along its angled stems that give it a texture closer to a small Hoodia than a typical smooth-stemmed Huernia. Its yellow flowers, patterned with fine wine-red zebra striping and a glossy raised ring at the mouth, appear near the base of the stems in warm weather. Grow it in bright light or light shade — too much direct sun can scald the bristled stems, while too little light produces weak, floppy growth and fewer flowers. Keep the fast-draining mix on the dry side, watering only once the soil has dried out fully.
sources: San Marcos Growers
Cactus and Succulent Society of America
University of California Cooperative Extension — Succulents

planting.note: Plant in full sun in coarse, mineral, extremely well-drained soil; this Madagascar native is among the most cold-sensitive Pachypodium species and should never be exposed to temperatures below 45-50°F. Water regularly through the growing season and reduce sharply in winter as the plant slows down.

directions: Pachypodium baronii develops a swollen, branching caudex covered in paired, reddish spines that mellow to brown with age, and it is the only species in the genus to bloom in true red rather than white, yellow, or pink. The trumpet-shaped flowers, each marked with a small white eye at the center, appear over a long season from spring into summer and last for several days apiece. Native to a narrow region of northwestern Madagascar, it is now rare and protected in the wild but has become a prized subject among caudiciform collectors in cultivation. Grow it in full sun with coarse, sharply draining soil, watering generously in summer while never letting the soil turn bone dry, and give it a warm, dry winter rest away from cold drafts.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online
Cactus and Succulent Society of America
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Pachypodium for indoor and outdoor culture

planting.note: Plant in full sun in gritty, sharply draining soil; give generous water and full light through the warm growing season, then cut back sharply in the cooler months as the plant goes dormant and drops its leaves.

directions: Pachypodium densiflorum forms a smooth, shining caudex that tapers gradually into several short, stout branches, creating a sculptural bonsai-like silhouette prized by caudiciform collectors. In spring it produces relatively large, deep golden-yellow flowers, each marked with a small white cone at the center, typically appearing before or alongside the new leaves. It is one of the more sun-tolerant Pachypodium species and grows best in full, unfiltered light even during the hottest part of summer. Keep the gritty mix on the dry side in winter, since the plant is naturally leafless and dormant during the cooler months and prone to rot if watered while resting.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online
Henry Shaw Cactus and Succulent Society

planting.note: Plant in full sun in well-drained, gritty soil; water sparingly through summer and keep completely dry in winter, since this South African species is intolerant of cold, wet conditions.

directions: Pachypodium bispinosum takes its name from the paired spines that stud its stems, and it forms a partly subterranean, tuberous caudex typical of the winter-deciduous pachypodiums native to South Africa's Eastern and Western Cape. Small, bell-shaped flowers in shades of purple to pink, sometimes with paler lobes, appear on the stems in the warmer months. It is naturally found among rocky, dry scrub and is more tolerant of cool nights than the Madagascar species, though it still cannot withstand frost or standing water. Grow it in full sun with excellent drainage, watering only during active summer growth and withholding water entirely while the plant is leafless and dormant in winter.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute — PlantZAfrica
Cactus and Succulent Society of America
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Propagate only from rooted offsets (pups) or tissue-cultured divisions, since seed-grown plants will not reliably retain the cream-striped variegation; pot in sharply drained, sandy soil and place in bright light, with some protection from the most intense midday sun to prevent leaf scorch on the lighter-colored stripes.

directions: Variegated Ponytail Palm is a slower-growing sport of the species with cream-to-yellow longitudinal stripes running the length of each narrow, arching leaf, prized by collectors for the contrast against its swollen, water-storing caudex base. Because the reduced chlorophyll in the pale stripes makes it more prone to leaf burn than the solid-green species, it generally does best with bright but slightly filtered light rather than the harshest full sun. Water deeply but infrequently, allowing the sandy, fast-draining soil to dry out completely between waterings, and protect it from temperatures below 40°F. Its variegation is stable when propagated vegetatively from pups or tissue culture, but plants grown from seed typically revert to solid green.
sources: Dave's Garden — Pony Tail Palms: An Introduction to Beaucarneas
World of Succulents
University of Florida IFAS Extension
